name: Victor Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Could you describe a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an electricity line crew that repairs the river crossings and high spans outside town. I have a two-year technical diploma and at 43 I'm trusted to decide whether the weather gives us a safe window. I enjoy finding a fault with a drone and then fixing it; the long drives and missed evenings with the children wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home, and how much AI do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works as a therapy assistant, and we have two children in school, a mortgage and about three months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for linework and there are some other utilities within reach. I use AI every day to sort inspection images and plan visits, then make the field crew confirm anything the screen marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the AI tools are modest but handy for sorting inspection photos. A drone can show a cracked crossarm; a worker still has to get to the power line and replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel secure enough on the repair crew. My partner's therapy assistant shifts are fairly regular, and our three months of expenses saved cover a brief gap, though the mortgage keeps us sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the river-crossing repair rota and use the image search I already run each morning. Once a week I'll compare its marked photos with the crew's close inspection notes, then fix any wrong label before the next patrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job and a bit amused that the grand claims turned into a better filing cabinet. I still like a tool that saves a walk to the wrong tower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a wrong photo label you caught.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The search once marked a shadow as rust on the west crossing. We sent the drone back at noon, saw clean metal and kept the bucket for an actual cracked fitting. An AI image search can mistake a shadow for rust; the noon drone photo showed clean metal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does three months saved let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months is enough for a short interruption, not a reason to buy every new device. We'd keep paying the mortgage and let the family holiday wait until the reserve grows.

say: **Drone photos** and AI sorting can help patrols, while workers still repair damaged power lines.
A useful **image search** is enough even if the bigger AI promises fade.
think: My **repair wage** and my partner's therapy shifts look stable in this mild picture.
Our **three-month reserve** covers a short gap, but the mortgage limits extra spending.
do: **Keep** the river-crossing repair rota and daily image search.
**Compare** weekly AI photo labels with close inspection notes before patrols.
feel: **Calm** about work, with ordinary care around mortgage spending.
S0.quote: An AI image search can mistake a shadow for rust; the noon drone photo showed clean metal.
fieldNote: He uses **AI every day** but checks flagged photos against close inspection.
Stable household shifts and a **three-month cushion** explain his mild-scenario calm about the repair job.

steps.text: Keep river-crossing repair rota and daily image search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that AI may take over route planning, buying and photo checking before a robot can repair a high crossing. I want our crew to test the new photo system on difficult spans, not just accept a neat screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on line repairs should remain, but the company may ask one lead worker to cover more towers with fewer inspectors. I can use the tools, yet a bigger patrol area could mean longer days away from the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll run the approved AI image checker on 50 old drone photos with known faults and count its misses. If the company accepts the result, I'll request paid time to teach the crew the checker and keep a log of travel hours for the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about workload, not convinced my wages would vanish. I like change that leaves enough time to climb and check properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you measure the checker on those 50 photos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd split the 50 photos between rust, cracked insulators and harmless shadows, then compare the machine's marks with the original repair sheets. A missed cracked power-line insulator belongs in the report, not under a good average score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new patrol area adds travel days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If travel days grow, I'd show the log to the supervisor and ask for a second crew rather than miss school nights indefinitely. I would not ask my partner to change therapy shifts to make up for a bad roster.

say: **Photo checking** and route planning may change before robots can repair high crossings.
A **50-photo test** should include dangerous misses, not just an average score.
think: My **line repairs** should remain, but a larger patrol area could lengthen days.
Longer **travel hours** would press on family time even if pay stays intact.
do: **Test** the approved image checker on 50 old drone photos with known faults.
**Request** paid crew instruction time if the company accepts the results.
feel: **Uneasy** about workload and family time, while expecting continued wages.
S1.quote: A missed cracked power-line insulator belongs in the report, not under a good average score.
fieldNote: His acceptance of AI rests on a **measured fault test** rather than enthusiasm alone.
The main risk he names is **travel time** after fewer inspectors cover more towers.

steps.text: Test approved AI checker on 50 known-fault drone photos

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could take route and inspection planning before the field robots arrive around 2031. A robot that repairs a high span could then reduce the number of lineworkers the company sends out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put myself forward to test the machines, but I cannot assume a testing post exists. Three months of savings and a mortgage mean a cut in my crew hours would reach home quickly, even if my partner's therapy shifts continue. Three months of savings will not make a cut in power-line crew hours harmless to our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask management for the 2028 planning changes and the 2031 line crew forecast. I'll request a paid field robot pilot if one opens, and from the next pay we'll put the monthly holiday deposit into the emergency account instead of booking travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can still name several moves. Losing a portion of crew hours would hurt; I do not expect to be dismissed tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear about the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children the holiday booking is delayed and that the mortgage is our first bill. I would not tell them that a robot has already taken my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the robot pilot useful to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pilot has to pay my normal wage and let me handle the safety controls. If it is only a viewing day, I would attend on company time but would not call it a new career.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes planning before capable field robots reach line repairs around 2031.
The company should publish **crew forecasts** before offering vague promises about new jobs.
think: I might fit a **pilot role**, but no paid testing vacancy is guaranteed.
A cut in **line hours** would reach our mortgage quickly with only three months saved.
do: **Ask** management for planning changes and the 2031 crew forecast.
**Join** a paid robot pilot if offered with normal wages and safety controls.
**Save** the monthly holiday deposit from new pay in our emergency account.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour cuts, with a practical route to test new equipment.
S2.quote: Three months of savings will not make a cut in power-line crew hours harmless to our mortgage.
fieldNote: He expects **planning work first** and field robot effects roughly three years later.
His pilot interest requires **normal pay** and control access, not a viewing day.
The holiday transfer is **new saving from pay** instead of a booking.

steps.text: Ask management for 2028 changes and 2031 crew forecast
Join paid robot pilot if offered with wages and safety controls
Save monthly holiday deposit from next pay in emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five-year picture gives enough time to build a serious field trial before robots work high spans around 2034. Thinking AI by 2031 will change the planning desk sooner; I can test that part while we prepare the climbing side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become the person who checks robot repairs, but the company might choose fewer lead lineworkers instead. Our three-month cushion gives us some control, not a promise that the mortgage would be easy after a long cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask to run the approved route planner on our next six crossing jobs and compare it with crew travel times. If a company-paid robot controls course is offered after a field trial, I'll enrol while keeping my lead lineworker roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the eventual crew shape and interested in the tests. Five years is long enough to find out whether the new work actually pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record on those six route jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare planned versus actual driving time and any missed access gate on each of the six jobs. A fast AI route on a map counts for nothing if our power-line crew misses the safe weather window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave your lead crew for inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a paid role with field checks and at least my normal roster hours before moving into robot inspection. Until there is a real offer, I'll keep leading line repairs.

say: **Six route jobs** can test thinking AI before field robots reach high crossings around 2034.
A future **robot inspection role** must carry real wages and field duties.
think: A new **inspection post** may suit me, but fewer lead workers is another possible outcome.
Our **three-month cushion** buys time to test, not safety through a long income cut.
do: **Compare** AI route plans with travel and access on six crossing jobs.
**Enrol** in a company-paid robot controls course if offered after a trial.
feel: **Anxious** about later crew numbers, but interested in evidence from field tests.
S3.quote: A fast AI route on a map counts for nothing if our power-line crew misses the safe weather window.
fieldNote: He tests **thinking AI now** because route planning changes before field robotics.
The controls course is an **actual conditional enrolment**, with company payment and a prior trial.
He keeps his **lead roster** until an inspection offer meets pay and duty conditions.

steps.text: Compare AI routes with travel and access on six crossing jobs
Enrol in company-paid robot controls course if offered after trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to train apprentices on both line tools and machine controls. Thinking AI by 2036 may plan crossings first; capable field robots around 2039 could then change the repair crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 56 at the robot date, and I might prefer to inspect difficult spans rather than climb them. That is a choice only if a paid post exists; my partner and I still have a mortgage, even if the children are older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my technical diploma skills current and learn each approved survey tool as the company introduces it. Every year we'll review mortgage balance and actual inspection vacancies before deciding whether I should leave the repair rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to make a ten-year plan, though I would miss climbing with my crew. The household has time to see real job offers before making a leap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice about a drone image?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show an apprentice a drone fault image and then take them to the same tower so they see what the camera missed. The trade will need people who know both views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection role real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a written offer with wages, travel demands and field authority before I move. A title on a future organisation chart is not a job I can budget around. A future organisation chart will not pay our mortgage; a written power-line inspection offer might.

say: **Apprentices** should learn both drone images and physical checks before robots arrive around 2039.
**2036 thinking AI** changes planning earlier than repair robots change field crews.
think: At **56**, I may want inspection work if a paid post is offered.
Our **mortgage** still needs a budget based on real wages, not an organisation chart.
do: **Keep** technical line skills current and learn approved survey tools as introduced.
**Review** paid inspection vacancies and mortgage balance each year before changing roles.
feel: **Calm** about having time to plan, with sadness about eventually leaving the climb.
S4.quote: A future organisation chart will not pay our mortgage; a written power-line inspection offer might.
fieldNote: He wants to keep **field authority** and pay visible in any later inspection move.
His ten-year path links **apprentice teaching** to both camera evidence and tower checks.

steps.text: Keep technical line skills current and learn approved survey tools
Review paid inspection vacancies and mortgage balance annually

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a capable field robot arriving around 2031 could cut our repair hours before I have proof of another paid role. A crew forecast and a paid field pilot with real controls would help me make a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person running a repair robot can stop it from the tower site. A lineworker's hand on a stop control matters more than a good demonstration video. I would only trust the new job after trying the controls myself. A lineworker's hand on a robot stop control matters more than a good demonstration video.

headlineQuote: A lineworker's hand on a robot stop control matters more than a good demonstration video.
portrait: **Victor**, 43, leads river-crossing power-line repairs and uses a technical diploma to judge safe weather windows.
He uses **AI daily** for drone images and routes, then has the field crew verify each marked fault.
His **mortgage**, two school-age children and three-month reserve limit how much lost crew time he could absorb.
He seeks **paid robot controls** and written inspection offers before changing his repair roster.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time before field robots around 2031 could reduce paid repair hours.
whatWouldHelp: A published **crew forecast** and paid field pilot with real safety controls would help him plan.
